title: The if Statement
description: Running some instructions only when a condition is true.

content.text: You only drive when the light is green. Until now every line of your program ran every time. An `if` lets a block run only when a condition is true.

parts.label: condition
parts.note: Round brackets around a question that is `true` or `false`.

parts.label: open brace
parts.note: The guarded block starts here and ends at the matching `}`.

content.title: Anatomy of an if line
content.caption: No semicolon at the end of this line: it ends with `{`.

steps.note: Is `75 > 50`? Yes, `true`. C++ enters the block.
This line is after the closing brace, outside the `if`. It always runs.

content.title: Follow the true path
content.outro: Change `score` to 30 and the guarded line is skipped. Only `Program finished.` is left.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `30 > 50` is false, so the block is skipped. The last line is outside the `if`, so it always runs.

items.text: A bool variable on its own
items.sub: `if (isAdult)` needs no comparison. Flip it with `!isAdult`.

content.title: What can go in the brackets

content.caption: `if (isAdult == true)` also works, but the `== true` adds nothing: `isAdult` is already the answer.

items.title: Not zero
items.text: 2 counts as true, so the block runs.

items.title: Zero
items.text: 0 counts as false, so the block is skipped.

content.title: Any number is a condition
content.caption: C++ treats 0 as false and every other number as true. This course writes `if (lives != 0)` because it is clearer, but you will meet the short form in other code.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `n` is 0, and 0 counts as false. The block is skipped and only `Done` prints.

content.value: The most famous bug in C++: writing `=` (store) where you meant `==` (compare). It compiles, because any number can be a condition.

steps.note: `lives = 1` does not ask anything. It **stores** 1 in `lives`, and that 1 is then used as the condition: true.
So the block runs, even though the player had 3 lives.

content.title: Two things go wrong at once
content.outro: `if (x = 5)` is always true, whatever `x` was before, and it wipes out the old value.

items.title: Always true
items.text: Stores 1 in `lives`, then treats 1 as true.

content.title: = stores, == asks
content.caption: Many compilers warn: `suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value`. When you see it, look for a missing `=`.

content.question: `int x = 0;` then `if (x = 5)`. Does the block run?
content.explain: `x = 5` stores 5, and 5 is not zero, so it counts as true. The block runs every time.

content.value: These also compile without any error, yet the program does the wrong thing.

content.caption: A score of 10 passed! The `;` right after the brackets ends the `if`, so it guards nothing. An `if` line ends with `{`, never `;`.

items.title: No braces
items.text: Only the first line is guarded. `Well done!` prints even for a score of 10.

items.title: Braces
items.text: Both lines are guarded. It costs two characters.

content.title: Always write the braces
content.caption: C++ ignores indentation. The braces are what decide which lines belong to the `if`.

content.question: With `score = 10`, what does the no-braces version print?
content.explain: Without braces only the first line after the `if` is guarded. The second line runs every time.

items: You can write as many `if` statements in a row as you like.
Each one is checked **on its own**, so several, one or none may run.
Use this when more than one answer can apply at once.

content.title: Every if gets its own turn
content.outro: Two of the three ran. When the answers are alternatives, like grades, you want `else` instead: that is the next lesson.

content.question: With `marks = 100`, how many lines does it print?
content.explain: All three conditions are true, and each `if` is checked separately, so all three blocks run.

practice.question: Ask for a temperature. If it is above 35, print: Stay indoors. Nothing should print for cooler temperatures.
Ask for an age and print: You may ride. only when the age is 12 or more AND under 60. Use one `if` with `&&`.
This prints You passed! even for a score of 10. Find the extra character that breaks it and remove it.
This says Last life! when the player has 3 lives, and it changes `lives` too. Fix the condition so it only asks the question.

quiz.question: What can go inside the round brackets of an `if`?
options: Something that gives true or false, or a number, where 0 counts as false
quiz.explain: Comparisons, logical expressions and bool variables are the normal choice. C++ also accepts a number: 0 is false and anything else is true.

quiz.question: What does `if (score >= 50);` followed by a block do?
options: Nothing is guarded: the semicolon ends the if, so the block always runs.
The block runs only when the score is 50 or more.
quiz.explain: The semicolon is an empty instruction, and that becomes the whole body of the `if`. The block after it is then just an ordinary block that always runs.

quiz.question: Without braces, how much of the following code belongs to an `if`?
options: Everything up to the next blank line
quiz.explain: C++ ignores indentation completely. Only one instruction is attached, which is why leaving the braces out is such a reliable source of bugs.

quiz.question: `int lives = 3;` What happens with `if (lives = 1) { ... }`?
options: It compares lives with 1, so the block is skipped.
It stores 1 in lives, and because 1 counts as true the block always runs.
quiz.explain: A single `=` assigns. The value 1 is then used as the condition, which is true. Use `==` to ask the question.

quiz.question: Three separate `if` statements are true at the same time. How many blocks run?
options: All three: each `if` is judged on its own.
quiz.explain: Independent `if` statements do not know about each other. When you want exactly one of several alternatives, you need `else`.
